$$
\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x+1} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \,\text{d}x=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\,{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\cdot x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{x}{x+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use a substitution $x+1=u,$ thus $x=u-1$ and $\text{d}x=\text{d}u.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{x}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \frac{u-1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-\int \,\text{d}u+\int \frac{\text{d}u}{u} \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-u+\operatorname{ln}⁡u+D \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-(x+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+D \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=D-1$ is an integral constant.

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}x(\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{log}_{5}⁡(({e}^{3})^{3})\,({e}^{3})-{log}_{5}⁡({1}^{3})\,(1)]-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3}{log}_{5}⁡({e}^{9})-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & ={e}^{3}\cdot \frac{9}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}({e}^{3}-1) \\  & =\frac{6{e}^{3}+3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{2}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}x(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(({e}^{3})^{2})\,({e}^{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2})\,(1)]-2{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{6})-2x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & =6{e}^{3}-2({e}^{3}-1) \\  & =4{e}^{3}+2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and $v',$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot 3{x}^{2}=\frac{3}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=4x\, & ⟹\,v=\int 4x\,\text{d}x=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}4x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{e}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot (2{x}^{2}){|}_{1}^{e}-{\int }_{1}^{e}(2{x}^{2})\cdot \frac{3}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[2{(e)}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{3})-2{(1)}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3})]-6{\int }_{1}^{e}x\text{d}x \\  & =6{e}^{2}-6(\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =6{e}^{2}-3{x}^{2}{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =6{e}^{2}-3({e}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{2}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing an Arbitrary Logarithm
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{4}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{4}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{4}⁡x(-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})-\int (-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,{log}_{4}⁡x+\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(-\,\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})+C \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C \\  & =-\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}{4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula $\log_4{x}=\dfrac{\ln{x}}{\ln{4}}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing a Single Logarithmic Factor
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
At first, it may not look like we have two factors. Actually, we do, but one of them is implicit. The trick is to write the integral as

$$
\int \ln{x}\,\textrm{d}x = \int \ln{x} \cdot 1 \cdot \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Using this trick, we can now use integration by parts. We let

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the by-parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+C \\  & =x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we want to evaluate the integral

$$
\int x\ln{x}\, \textrm{d}x \,.
$$

The method of integration by parts can help us solve this problem. Let's remind ourselves of the "by-parts" formula,

$$
\int u v' \textrm{d}x = uv - \int v u'\textrm{d}x.
$$

We usually let $u = x,$ but that would leave us with $v' = \ln(x)$ which is hard to integrate. So instead, we're going to choose our $u$ and $v'$ slightly differently, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now the formula of integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int {{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}_{⏟}}_{u}\cdot {{x}_{⏟}}_{{v}^{′}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}-\int \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{2}\int x\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

When we apply integration by parts to integrals containing logarithmic functions, we should *always* identify the logarithmic function with $u,$ not with $v'.$
